correctness.rationale: Use intrinsic shortest paths, not those of the ambient lattice. The same-color displacement vectors of length two are ±e1, ±e2, ±(e1-e2); their adjacency around a vertex is a six-cycle, giving two translation types of triangles, centered and alternating. A same-color pair has a unique midpoint by the absence of 4-cycles. In the alternating type the three midpoints are distinct and form, with the triple, an elementary hexagon; any 6-cycle must be of this type. A mixed clique with two vertices in each color would give a 4-cycle, and all other mixed cliques belong to one closed-neighborhood simplex. Deleting bonds or vertices cannot make new cliques and the three required midpoint paths certify that an exceptional triangle survives exactly with its whole face. In the centered core, pair a face of at least two neighbors with its cone from the center, in decreasing face size. The unique midpoint prohibits competing cofaces from other centered simplices; this collapses the core relative to G, not the full complex. Each exceptional triangular attaching loop becomes the original six-edge loop via midpoint paths, giving two disks per face. The first disks fill disjoint face interiors in the plane. A finite nonempty set of such faces has a boundary edge incident to only one remaining face (e.g. an extreme face in a lattice direction), so these disks can be collapsed one by one, each with one edge. The remainder is a connected graph with rank b-h, including the tree/single-vertex cases. The exact relative homology sequence gives the primitive rank-h boundary kernel: the relative 2-chains for the first disks inject because the planar filling has zero H_2, and the quotient H_1 is the free group in homology of the remaining graph. Each second attaching loop is null after the first disks and adds one S^2. This proves the integral map and wedge type, not only Betti numbers; a nonbridge deletion changes (b,h) to (b-1,h-t) with the metric recomputed. value.rationale: This is a complete defect-tolerant topology calculation for a natural lattice, not an extrapolation from intact polyhexes. It identifies the actual cycles killed over the integers and explains the local but counterintuitive transition under a shared-bond loss: two 2-spheres disappear while a 1-cycle is created. The result gives a computable classification without convexity, inducedness or non-overlap assumptions.
